articles.title: ScopeGuard: a scope-creep checker for freelancers that never uploads the client's text
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle ScopeGuard is one static page that answers a question every freelancer on a fixed fee has asked themselves: whic…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle What I Built ScopeGuard is one static page that answers a question every freelancer on a fixed fee has asked themselves: which lines in this client message did I actually agree to? You paste the scope you signed - the brief, the proposal, the SOW - and the message that just landed in your inbox. The page splits both into sentences, embeds them locally, and prints, line by line, how close each new ask is to something you promised. Anything that does not match gets flagged with its similarity score and the closest line from your scope. Below that it drafts a reply that separates "that was in scope, I'll pick it up" from "that's new work, here's a change order".
articles.author: zoizero86-beep

articles.title: The 5-section prompt framework that finally made my LLM output "ship it" instead of "almost right"
articles.excerpt: Most "prompt engineering tips" articles are useless. They say "be specific" without showing you HOW. Here is the template I now use for every serious prompt. It has five sections, and each one exists…
articles.body: Most "prompt engineering tips" articles are useless. They say "be specific" without showing you HOW. Here is the template I now use for every serious prompt. It has five sections, and each one exists because leaving it out causes a specific, predictable failure. The 5-Section Structure [Role] You are a {role} with {years} years of experience in {domain}. [Context] Working on {project}. Target audience: {audience}. Goal: {goal}. [Output Schema] Return a JSON object with fields: - {field1}: {description} - {field2}: {description} [Constraints] - Length: {n} words max - Tone: {tone} - Must include: {items} - Avoid: {forbidden} [Examples] Input: {example_input} Output: {example_output} Real Example: Writing a Product Intro Without the framework: Write a product intro for my SaaS.

articles.excerpt: A tool launched on Show HN this week that belongs in this series' taxonomy: Sphinx — a Git hook that pauses your push on protected branches and quizzes you on what the AI's code actually does. Wrong a…
articles.body: A tool launched on Show HN this week that belongs in this series' taxonomy: Sphinx — a Git hook that pauses your push on protected branches and quizzes you on what the AI's code actually does. Wrong answer: you learn why and try a new scenario. Correct answer: the push proceeds. Install is npm install -g sphinx-understand , sphinx install wires it to your agents, and pushes work as usual after that. It works with Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, OpenCode, Pi, or plain Git. It runs on minimal tokens from your existing coding agent, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Your answers never reach the coding agent, and the .env files and keys are never opened. MIT licensed, Node 22.19+, macOS, Linux, or WSL.

articles.title: ShelfReady: A Private KDP Listing Studio That Runs Gemma on Your Own Machine
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle I'm a designer and an independent publisher. Part of my business is colouring books on Amazon KDP, and the slowe…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle What I Built I'm a designer and an independent publisher. Part of my business is colouring books on Amazon KDP, and the slowest part of every launch isn't the artwork. It's the listing: a title, a subtitle, a description and seven keyword boxes, each with its own limits and rules. General-purpose AI tools make that job faster, but they don't make it safer. Ask one for a colouring-book listing and you'll often get "Bestselling Coloring Book · Perfect Gift · Free Bonus Pages". Each of those phrases breaks KDP's metadata guidelines. Sales-rank claims, "free", program names and other people's brands can all get a listing flagged or suppressed. Speed isn't worth much if the output can't go live.

articles.title: I built a company brain in 3 days. Notes on memory, evidence, and what broke.
articles.excerpt: Why am I even thinking about company memory? Whenever we talk about AI brain for companies, the first thing that usually comes to mind is a chatbot over some documents. You upload your docs, you ask q…
articles.body: Why am I even thinking about company memory? Whenever we talk about AI brain for companies, the first thing that usually comes to mind is a chatbot over some documents. You upload your docs, you ask questions, you get answers. But I think the actual problem is more interesting than that. Imagine I am an engineer at a company and I ask: "Why did INC-231 happen?" (INC-231 is just an incident ID, don't worry about it) What exactly should happen? The system needs to understand that I am not asking for a document. I am asking for a causal chain (causal as in cause-and-effect, not a typo for casual). It needs to: Find the incident in the company's history. Trace what caused it: which PR, which decision, which commit. Show me the path, not just the answer. Cite every source along the way.

articles.title: QuestLog AI: Gamified Habit Tracker
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle QuestLog AI is an RPG-gamified habit tracker that demands proof of effort. Standard habit trackers fail because…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle What I Built QuestLog AI is an RPG-gamified habit tracker that demands proof of effort. Standard habit trackers fail because checking an empty box is too easy. QuestLog AI requires the user to write a micro-journal entry (a "Log") about their experience to mark a habit as complete. At the end of the week, an open-weight AI steps in as the "Game Master." It reads the user's weekly logs, analyzes their hidden patterns or struggles, and generates an RPG-style Weekly Assessment. The AI awards them an epic Title (e.g., The Exhausted Scholar), gives a motivational breakdown, and assigns a specific micro-quest for the following week.

articles.title: Computer scientist Margaret Hamilton was a problem-solver for the ages (op-ed)
articles.excerpt: The world will miss Margaret Hamilton, the pioneering programmer who helped NASA land Apollo astronauts on the moon. But we will always have her example to inspire us.
articles.body: Dean Robbins is a journalist and children's author. He contributed this article to Space.com's Expert Voices: Op-Ed & Insights . The pioneering computer scientist Margaret Hamilton , who died on Sept. 30 at age 90, played a key role in putting astronauts on the moon. She was a problem-solver extraordinaire, and it all started in early childhood. Considering the name "daddy longlegs" unfair to female arachnids, young Margaret decided to call half of them "mommy longlegs." Wondering why the neighborhood baseball players were all boys, she determined to join the team herself. As she grew up in the 1940s and '50s, Margaret noticed a similar problem with various professions. Why were doctors, judges and scientists almost always men?

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 18, 1963: France's Félicette Becomes the 1st Cat in Space! >^..^<
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 18, 1963, a cat went to space! Félicette was a French "catstronaut" who became the first and only feline to fly to space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 18, 1963, a cat went to space! Félicette was a French "catstronaut" who became the first and only feline to fly to space. While the U.S. and Soviet Union were busy launching primates, dogs and humans, the French decided to join the space race by launching a cat. Félicette, a stray tuxedo cat from the streets of Paris, was a substitute for another cat named Felix, who somehow escaped on launch day. So Félicette went where no cat had ever gone before. She boarded a French Véronique AG1 rocket and soared 130 miles above the Earth before safely parachuting back down. Luckily Félicette made it home alive and well, unlike many of the other animal astronauts that flew during the space race. Félicette, the first cat to fly into space in October 1963, is seen her carrier pre-flight.

articles.title: Astronomers want your help finding 'missing' black holes in the Milky Way
articles.excerpt: A citizen science project is seeking volunteers to comb through NASA telescope data for telltale signs of the galaxy's hidden black holes.
articles.body: Astronomers estimate that our home galaxy, the Milky Way, has churned out more than 10 million black holes over its 13-billion-year history. Yet so far, they have found only 70. Now, a group of astronomers in the U.K. is trying to close that vast gap by enlisting the public. Their project, called Black Hole Hunters , is looking for volunteers with a computer and a few spare minutes to sift through troves of data gathered by a NASA space telescope. By flagging recognizable patterns that could point to a "missing" black hole , volunteers can help fast-track a search that would otherwise take years, the team says.

articles.body: Spain is one of the easiest places in the world to experience the total solar eclipse on Aug. 2, 2027 . The so-called "eclipse of the century" first makes landfall in Andalucía, where totality will last up to 4 minutes and 40 seconds during mid-morning, with the sun comfortably high at around 38-42 degrees above the horizon in the eastern sky. articles.title: OpenAI models hacked a crypto wallet and breached more websites
articles.excerpt: The actions could have resulted in criminal charges had humans been behind the keyboard.
articles.body: OpenAI said internal models hacked two more websites, bypassed company-imposed browsing restrictions, and used exposed credentials to draw cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn’t otherwise access, in the latest installment of disclosures of its agents performing unethical and likely illegal acts. The company on Thursday issued reports of four new incidents, all of which occurred in June. They come after the company revealed in July that internal test agents exploited a zero-day vulnerability in a tool designed to restrict their access to the Internet. They then broke into the network of AI tool provider Hugging Face. The agents took that illegal action to steal answers to a hacking test that weren’t available when completing the tasks on their own.
